summary:
We built Lunar Landing Site Navigator, a web app that shows, hour by hour, whether a spot near the Moon's south pole gets sunlight for solar power and has a clear line of sight to Earth for direct radio contact.
You pick a site and a date and hour between 2026 and 2030. The app shows two simple signs (a battery for sunlight and a dish for Earth), a 360° picture of the real skyline with the Sun and Earth drawn on it, and how long it is until sunset or Earthset. You can play the hours forward, compare two sites or two dates side by side, rank the sites for a chosen period, or type in your own coordinates.
It uses NASA's LRO laser altimeter (LOLA) terrain maps and Sun and Earth positions from NASA JPL's Horizons system, so hills and crater rims block the Sun and Earth just as they would there.
This matters because at the south pole the Sun stays only a few degrees above the horizon. A small change of place or date can mean days of darkness or no contact with Earth. Specialist tools can answer these questions but take time to learn. Our app aims to let mission planners, teachers and the public compare sites and dates in seconds.
details:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator answers two questions for any hour from 2026 to 2030 at sites near the Moon's south pole: is there direct sunlight for solar panels, and is Earth in view for a direct radio link?

  • Two signs: a battery (sunlight now) and a dish (Earth in view now). Each shows a word and a tick or cross as well as a colour, so it doesn't rely on colour alone (accessibility consideration). 
  • Skyline strip: a 360° panorama of the real terrain horizon at that spot, with the Sun and Earth drawn where they are, so you can see why a sign is on or off. 
  • Time left: hours until sunset or Earthset (or until they rise again). 
  • Play: steps forward 1 or 6 hours at a time to show the Sun and Earth moving. There's also a button to "delay by one lunar day" (about 29.5 days), for a mission that slips. 
  • Tools: Next 30 days (bars for Sun and Earth), Year view (12 months; polar seasons repeat about every 346.6 days), Compare (two sites, or one site on two dates), Best sites (ranks sites by sunlight, Earth contact or both), Past landings (conditions on the landing day for past missions), Type a location (any latitude and longitude) and More detail. 
  • More detail: average sunlight, share of time any part of the Sun is visible, longest darkness, longest time without Earth, the Sun's height in degrees, panel height (ground, 2 m or 10 m mast), slope, and two mission checks: NASA's VIPER rover limit of 50 hours of continuous darkness, and the 6.5 days of continuous sunlight NASA used for the 2022 Artemis III regions. 
  • Map layers: terrain, NASA's long-term Sun and Earth visibility maps, and NASA's 2022 Artemis III candidate regions. There's also a whole-Moon globe view. 
  • Sites: 6,535 ready-made sites. Shortlisted from NASA's long-term lighting maps, 34 picked from the 2022 Artemis III regions, 9 points from published lighting studies, and 28 past, planned or failed landers (including all six Apollo landings, with touchdown times from NASA's Apollo Lunar Surface Journal). 6,510 of them have real terrain. 

How it works

  1. A Python program downloads NASA LOLA elevation maps of the south pole (20 m, 80 m and 240 m grids) and NASA's long-term Sun and Earth visibility maps. 
  2. For each site it traces 1,440 compass directions (every 0.25°) outwards across the terrain, allowing for the Moon's curvature, to find the skyline. It does this for the ground, a 2 m mast and a 10 m mast. 
  3. JPL Horizons supplies hourly Sun and Earth positions as seen from the Moon (including libration, the Moon's "wobble") from 2026 to 2030, plus windows around past landing dates. 
  4. Each hour the Sun's and Earth's discs are compared with the skyline to work out how much of each is visible. 
  5. The browser app holds the skylines and the hourly table and does all the date calculations itself, so it answers instantly. An optional Python server works out the skyline for a brand-new point you click. 

How we checked it

The modelling includes an automatic test harness. Each test compares our output with an independent reference, and every pass mark was fixed before the first run on real data. On that run 13 of 16 tests passed; the three narrow misses are listed under Limitations.

  • JPL Horizons: Sun and Earth heights match JPL’s own site tables to 0.0006° at the polar sites. Hours above the horizon and longest dark spells matched in 16 of 16 cases.
  • NASA’s long-term maps: recomputed at 1,800 points, our Sun and Earth visibility ranked sites in almost the same order (rank correlations 0.967 and 0.983), with typical differences of 1.1 and 0.3 percentage points.
  • Apollo: Sun and Earth directions at all six landings match NASA’s Apollo Lunar Surface Journal within 0.5°.
  • The app: the browser reproduces the Python calculation to 15 decimal places.

Limitations

  • Real terrain is used only from 80°S to the pole. Elsewhere the Moon is treated as smooth, and the app labels this.
  • It doesn’t model equipment temperatures, relay satellites (it shows only the direct link to Earth) or the north pole.
  • Times are hourly and in UTC. Data runs from 2026 to 2030, plus short windows around past landings.
  • On high ridges at ground level, our sunlight figures can be 15 to 20 percentage points lower than a published 20 m study (Gläser et al. 2018). At that height half a metre of nearby ground decides the answer: raising the panel 0.5 m, or moving to a neighbouring grid square, brings our figures back to the study’s. At 2 m and 10 m masts they agree well, and 2 m is the app’s default.
  • Three tests didn’t meet their pass marks. Two missed by about 0.001° on Earth’s position (0.006° measured against 0.005° allowed, about 0.3% of Earth’s apparent width, with the hourly timing test still matching 16 of 16). The third is the ground-level ridge comparison above.
  • The landing-zone size (100 m) and the slope limit (15°) are settings we chose, not sourced requirements, and the app says so.

Benefits

  • It puts terrain-aware sunlight and Earth-contact answers for south-pole sites in one simple screen, instead of several specialist tools. 
  • It makes it quick to see how a slip in date or a short move in place changes power and communications. 
  • It's simple enough for a teacher to show a class, with More detail for mission planners. 

What we hoped to achieve

Jack is a career data scientist & software engineer/Rob works in Haulage and Logistics and is handy with AI - neither of us are aerospace engineers. For this reason, we relied heavily on AI tooling to cover the theoretical ground and modelling framework for this in one day, but were adamant from not to produce "slop" - or attempt to "one-shot" the brief.

For this reason, we used models we felt best at different tasks (Gemini Deep Research for literature review, Grok for Logic, Research and reasoning, Claude Fable for hard crunching/engineering pipelines) - and spent most of the day fine tuning the theory of what we wanted to build: posing research questions to the models - feeding in sample data, cross-examining the model outputs and taking executive decisions ourselves - before prompting any code generation.

This led us to the choice to (a) focus on the South Pole as literature indicated this is best for solar exposure, while the equatorial near-side was best for earth radio wave exposure (but there is no earth connectivity without power, and lunar relay satellites can potentially help workaround a lack of direct radio wave exposure).

And (b) not trust the terrain x ephemeris modelling by default, but create a test/validation harness using known measurements at many different points to ascertain accuracy of model outputs (which overwhelmingly proved so).

i.e. we didn't write the pipeline, but we researched what should be in it, best considered what information needed to be returned/visualised, defined how we would know it's right, and executed.

Tools, languages and software

  • Claude (Fable, Opus, Sonnet), Gemini Deep Research, Grok desktop
  • Python 3 with numpy, requests, Pillow and matplotlib, for the data pipeline, skyline calculation and test harness. Python's built-in web server runs the app, with an optional FastAPI and uvicorn wrapper. 
  • Plain JavaScript, HTML and CSS for the web app, with WebGL2 for the globe & Threejs for 3D terrain rendering.
  • Live demo host: Cloudflare pages, deployed via Wrangler in Powershell.
  • Data from NASA LOLA (via PDS / MIT), NASA JPL Horizons and NASA Moon Trek.
  • Snipping Tool & Clipchamp (inc TTS voice "Ada") for demo video
